lead: A block cipher such as AES encrypts one block: 128 bits. Real messages are longer or shorter. A mode of operation uses the block cipher repeatedly to encrypt any length. It decides padding, chaining, and where a changing value (IV or counter) enters. A bad choice leaks patterns or destroys secrecy. Every secure connection uses one of these modes.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.4 for what a block cipher is and Chapter 3.6 for AES, whose 128-bit block is assumed in every example here.

sections.h3: ECB: no chaining, and why that leaks

blocks.text: A block cipher E_K takes one n-bit plaintext block and key K, returns n ciphertext bits. AES has n = 128. E_K is a permutation; D_K reverses it. The cipher knows nothing about messages longer or shorter than one block.
A mode of operation supplies the rule. It fixes padding, treatment of each block, and the changing value (IV or counter) that makes two encryptions of the same block under the same key differ.

Electronic Codebook (ECB): Cᵢ = E_K(Pᵢ), block by block. Fast and fully parallel, but leaks: equal plaintext blocks become equal ciphertext blocks. Encrypt a bitmap and the picture's outline shows. A salary table with many 30000 rows repeats.

Padding for ECB is usually PKCS#7: append k bytes, each holding k, where k = 16 − (length mod 16) in bytes. If length is a multiple of 16, add a full block of sixteen bytes each value 16, so the receiver always finds a nonzero last byte.

sections.h3: CBC: chaining blocks with an IV

blocks.text: Cipher Block Chaining XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting it. The first block has no previous ciphertext, so it uses a stand-in block called the initialisation vector.

blocks.where: Cᵢ is ciphertext block i, Pᵢ is plaintext block i, K is the key, E_K is the block cipher, IV is the initialisation vector (one random block of n bits), and ⊕ is bitwise XOR. Decryption is Pᵢ = D_K(Cᵢ) ⊕ Cᵢ₋₁, again with C₀ = IV.

blocks.text: Two identical plaintext blocks now encrypt differently unless the preceding ciphertexts match, so the ECB leak disappears.

IV rules: the IV is not secret, travels with the ciphertext, but must be fresh, random, and unpredictable for every message under one key. Reuse an IV and the first blocks of two messages XOR with the same value, so matching plaintext prefixes show up. If an attacker can choose the IV, they set IV = G ⊕ X, where X is a known input block whose output C* was seen, and check whether the first ciphertext block equals C*. If equal, P₁ = G.

CBC encrypts serially, because block i needs Cᵢ₋₁. Decryption is parallel: D_K(Cᵢ) needs only Cᵢ, and Cᵢ₋₁ is already in hand. The last short block needs padding. One flipped bit in Cᵢ garbles all of Pᵢ and flips the same-position bit in Pᵢ₊₁; later blocks are unaffected.

sections.h3: CFB, OFB and CTR: turning the block cipher into a keystream

blocks.text: These three modes use the block cipher to generate keystream, then XOR. No padding is needed, because plaintext is consumed bit by bit or byte by byte.

Cipher Feedback (CFB): C₀ = IV and Cᵢ = E_K(Cᵢ₋₁) ⊕ Pᵢ. Ciphertext is fed back into the cipher. Decryption also runs E_K, never D_K. Encryption is serial, and a transmission error in Cᵢ garbles Pᵢ plus a few blocks until the error leaves the shift register.

Output Feedback (OFB): O₀ = IV, Oᵢ = E_K(Oᵢ₋₁), Cᵢ = Pᵢ ⊕ Oᵢ. The keystream depends only on key and IV, never on the message, so one flipped ciphertext bit flips exactly one plaintext bit. No parallelism, and reusing the IV repeats the whole keystream.

Counter mode (CTR): with nonce and counter, set Tᵢ = nonce ‖ (counter + i), Cᵢ = Pᵢ ⊕ E_K(Tᵢ). ‖ is concatenation. The counter starts at an agreed value (often 0 or 1) and increments per block. Encryption and decryption are the same XOR. Blocks are independent, so both directions run in parallel and any block can be read directly.

Counter rules: under one key, the input to E_K must never repeat. A nonce reused across two messages, or a counter that wraps around, produces the same keystream block twice, and then Cᵢ ⊕ Cᵢ′ = Pᵢ ⊕ Pᵢ′ for the same position i in the two messages. That is the one-time pad failure described in Chapter 3.2.

blocks.text: CBC and CTR cover most needs. CBC is older and still everywhere; CTR suits hardware, random access and parallel disks, and authenticated modes build on it. All five give confidentiality only. An attacker who flips ciphertext bits changes plaintext predictably, so integrity needs a MAC, which is Unit 4. See Chapter 3.9 for attack games.

figure.caption: CBC with the toy cipher E_K(x) = x ⊕ 1010, IV = 0000, P₁ = 1100 and P₂ = 0110. The second block XORs with C₁ before encryption, so C₂ depends on both plaintext blocks.

spec.title: CBC mode with two blocks
spec.aria: The first plaintext block is XORed with the IV and encrypted to C1; the second plaintext block is XORed with C1 and encrypted to C2, showing the chaining.

examples.question: A 4-bit toy block cipher is E_K(x) = x ⊕ K with key K = 1010, and D_K is the same operation. Use CBC mode with IV = 0000 to encrypt the two-block message P₁ = 1100, P₂ = 0110. Find C₁ and C₂, give the ciphertext, compare with ECB, and decrypt to verify.
steps: Given: K = 1010, IV = C₀ = 0000, P₁ = 1100, P₂ = 0110. All 4 bits.
ECB comparison: ECB gives E_K(1100) = 0110 and E_K(0110) = 1100, so ECB ciphertext is 0110 1100. If P₁ = P₂ = 1100, ECB would output 0110 0110 with two equal blocks; CBC would not.
Decrypt block 1: P₁ = D_K(C₁) ⊕ C₀ = (0110 ⊕ 1010) ⊕ 0000 = 1100. Recovered.
Decrypt block 2: P₂ = D_K(C₂) ⊕ C₁ = (1010 ⊕ 1010) ⊕ 0110 = 0110. Recovered, so the round trip is correct.
examples.answer: C₁ = 0110 (decimal 6) and C₂ = 1010 (decimal 10), so the ciphertext is 0110 1010; decryption returns P₁ = 1100 (12) and P₂ = 0110 (6).
examples.check:
K = 0b1010
IV = 0b0000
P1 = 0b1100
P2 = 0b0110
E = lambda x: x ^ K
D = E
C1 = E(P1 ^ IV)
C2 = E(P2 ^ C1)
print(C1)
print(C2)
print(D(C1) ^ IV)
print(D(C2) ^ C1)

traps: ECB is unsafe for messages longer than one block: equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks. Examiners like the case where a 16-byte block repeats and the ECB ciphertext shows it.
The IV is not a secret key. It is public, but must be fresh, random, and unpredictable for every message under one key.
A CTR nonce or counter must never repeat under one key. Repetition is one-time pad reuse: Cᵢ ⊕ Cᵢ′ = Pᵢ ⊕ Pᵢ′, so the plaintexts leak.
Only ECB and CBC need padding. CFB, OFB and CTR XOR a keystream and take any length.
In CBC a bit error in Cᵢ destroys all of Pᵢ and flips one bit in Pᵢ₊₁, then stops. Saying the error spreads to all later blocks is wrong.

quiz.q: What is an IV in CBC mode, and is it kept secret?
quiz.a: IV is a random block used as C₀. It is sent with ciphertext, not secret; must be unique and unpredictable for each message under one key.

quiz.q: Why does ECB reveal the structure of a message?
quiz.a: ECB computes Cᵢ = E_K(Pᵢ) with no dependence on earlier blocks. Same plaintext block and key always give same ciphertext block, so equal blocks and repeated patterns stay equal.

quiz.q: For the toy cipher E_K(x) = x ⊕ K, K = 1111, CBC with IV = 1010 and P₁ = 0011, compute C₁.
CTR mode with the toy cipher E_K(x) = x ⊕ K, K = 1010, uses nonce ‖ counter = 0000 for block 1 and P₁ = 1010. What is C₁?
quiz.a: Keystream block = E_K(0000) = 0000 ⊕ 1010 = 1010. C₁ = P₁ ⊕ keystream = 1010 ⊕ 1010 = 0000.

quiz.q: CBC decryption runs in parallel but CBC encryption does not. Explain, using the formulas.
quiz.a: Encryption: Cᵢ = E_K(Pᵢ ⊕ Cᵢ₋₁), so block i waits for Cᵢ₋₁: serial. Decryption: Pᵢ = D_K(Cᵢ) ⊕ Cᵢ₋₁, uses only received Cᵢ and Cᵢ₋₁, both available, so all blocks decrypt at once.

quiz.q: An implementer uses the same CTR nonce for two messages P and P′ under one key. Show what an attacker learns.
quiz.a: Both messages use the same keystream Sᵢ = E_K(nonce ‖ counter+i). Cᵢ = Pᵢ ⊕ Sᵢ and Cᵢ′ = Pᵢ′ ⊕ Sᵢ, so Cᵢ ⊕ Cᵢ′ = Pᵢ ⊕ Pᵢ′. The keystream cancels and the attacker sees the XOR of the two plaintexts, enough to recover both for text.

quiz.q: Why do CFB, OFB and CTR need no padding?
quiz.a: They are keystream modes: plaintext is XORed with generated keystream, bit by bit, so the last partial block simply uses fewer keystream bits. ECB and CBC must feed whole blocks into E_K, so they pad.

beyond: Not for exam. Real systems rarely use these modes raw: AES-GCM combines CTR with a polynomial MAC, AES-CCM combines CTR with CBC-MAC. Disk encryption uses XTS, a CBC-like mode that tweaks the key per sector so identical sectors differ. CTR fails on nonce reuse, so research moved to nonce-misuse-resistant modes such as AES-GCM-SIV. Search for AES-GCM, XTS, nonce-misuse-resistant encryption.
